title: "I Have to Fight": Indian Flydubai Captain Recounts Cockpit Axe Attack
excerpt: Captain Smit Machchhar, 35, of Ahmedabad describes staying conscious through a crash-axe attack, opening the cockpit door as FZ1073 fell 7,000 feet, and the investigations now under way in India and the UAE.
body:
• Flydubai Captain Smit Machchhar, 35, from Ahmedabad, has described how his co-pilot attacked him with a crash axe aboard Dubai-Tel Aviv flight FZ1073 on September 30.
  • Struck on the head and hands and drifting in and out of consciousness, Machchhar opened the cockpit door so crew and passengers could restrain the attacker while the jet fell about 7,000 feet in under a minute.
  • Off-duty pilots aboard restored control and diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia; everyone on board survived and the co-pilot was arrested.
  • India's NIA has registered a case under the Anti-Hijacking Act and UAPA, and the UAE Attorney General is running a parallel investigation.

An Indian flydubai captain has given his first detailed account of the mid-air attack that nearly brought down a Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight, describing how he fought to stay conscious after his own co-pilot struck him with the cockpit crash axe. Captain Smit Machchhar, 35, from Ahmedabad in Gujarat, recounted the September 30 attack aboard flight FZ1073 in a video interaction shared on October 17, according to India Today's report.

"Only One Thought in My Head"

Machchhar said the flight had been routine, with clear weather, before First Officer Hammam Al Hammami, a 34-year-old Omani national, told him he wished to pray. When Machchhar turned to his system display, Al Hammami took the emergency crash axe and struck him on the back of the head and then on his hands. Machchhar lost consciousness briefly, fought back as the blows continued, and realised the aircraft was descending fast.

https://x.com/CNNnews18/status/2111440963809796234

"I wasn't scared at that moment. Only one thought in my head: I have to fight this man and open that door."

— Captain Smit Machchhar

With the jet having fallen nearly 7,000 feet in under a minute and its speed climbing from 290 to 470 knots, Machchhar entered the cockpit door code and shouted for help. Passengers and cabin crew rushed in and restrained Al Hammami. A flydubai first officer who had been sitting in the cockpit and an Israir captain travelling as a passenger then restored control and diverted the aircraft to Tabuk in Saudi Arabia. Machchhar, drifting in and out of consciousness, kept repeating one instruction to himself: "If I fall asleep, it'll all be over. I have to stay awake, no matter what."

A Pilot's Career, a Family's Vigil

Machchhar began flying with IndiGo in 2010 and joined flydubai in 2019, building more than 16 years of experience. He is recovering in Abu Dhabi, where India's embassy in the UAE says he continues to make steady progress and its officials remain in contact with his family, doctors and local authorities. His brother Vishal, a serving Indian Air Force officer, said the family has supported him since childhood and continues to do so.

"He wasn't a terrorist. He was my co-pilot. I shared coffee with him, I shared food with him. We used to talk. I trusted him."

— Captain Smit Machchhar

Two Investigations, One Open Question

The National Investigation Agency has registered a case to examine a possible larger conspiracy, filing its FIR on October 9 under Section 3 of the Anti-Hijacking Act, 2016 and the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, according to The Hindu BusinessLine. The FIR records that flight 1073 left Dubai at 7.05 am GMT on September 30 with 174 passengers and six crew, dived rapidly near the Jordan-Saudi Arabia border at about 9.21 am GMT, and landed at Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz Airport in Tabuk at 10.45 am GMT, where Saudi authorities arrested the first officer. The UAE Attorney General, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, has opened a parallel investigation, and Al Hammami remains in custody. What motivated a trusted colleague to attack his captain remains the central unanswered question for both probes — and for cockpit security rules worldwide.
